study type: Cross-sectional correlational study using national database and expert survey
exposure: Environment for midwifery practice and interprofessional collaboration (scope of practice, autonomy, governance, prescriptive authority, restrictions affecting patient safety, quality, and access)
outcome: Access to care across birth settings
cohort: The study analyzed outcomes for births across all 50 US states from the CDC-Vital Statistics Database and surveyed 92 state regulatory experts to inform the Midwifery Integration Scoring system.
finding: Higher Midwifery Integration Scoring (MISS) scores in US states were significantly associated with higher rates of physiologic birth, less obstetric interventions, and fewer adverse neonatal outcomes, even after controlling for racial demographics.
mod_finding: Higher midwifery integration was associated with significantly higher rates of spontaneous vaginal delivery and vaginal birth after cesarean, and significantly lower rates of cesarean.
cross-section timing: The study correlated Midwifery Integration Scores (developed from regulatory data and expert survey) with outcomes from the CDC-Vital Statistics Database, reflecting a snapshot of conditions and outcomes across US states at the time of the study (published 2018).
